﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾. It has been said: this is from the words of Abraham, meaning: if you deny me, then this has happened to others before you. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him, meaning: if you deny Muhammad, then that is the custom of the disbelievers with those who came before. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ to his people to whom he was sent, and it is not incumbent upon him to guide them, nor is that within his capacity.

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ Al-Jumhur read "awa-lam yaraw" with the yā' (third person), as a report; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is as if he said: "Have the nations not seen?"

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbit, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the tā' (second person) as an address from Abraham to his people. It has also been said that it is an address from Allah to the Quraysh.

Al-Jumhur read "kayfa yubdi'" with a damma on the yā', from abda'a yubdi'u. Al-Zubayri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha, from bada'a yabda'u.

al-Zuhri read "kayfa bada'a," and the meaning is: have they not seen how Allah creates them originally, a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then breathes the spirit into it, then brings it out into the world, then causes it to die afterward? Likewise all animals and all plants. So when you see Allah's power over origination and bringing into being, He is the one able to repeat it. The hamza is for denying that they have not seen, and the waw is for coordination with an implied clause. ﴿Indeed that, for Allah, is easy﴾, because when He wills a matter, He says to it "Be," and it is.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded Abraham to tell his people to travel in the land, (p-1117) so that they might reflect and take heed. He said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation"﴾, with their multitude, diversity of colors, natures and languages. And look at the dwelling places of the past generations and the extinct nations and their remains, so that by this you may know the perfection of Allah's power.

It has also been said that the meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, "Travel." The meaning of His saying ﴿Then Allah produces the final creation﴾ is that Allah who began the first creation and created it in that manner will produce it a second time at the resurrection. The clause is coordinated with the clause "travel through the earth," and both are within the scope of "say." The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read "al-nash'ah" with a short vowel and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a long vowel and a fatha on the shin; both are dialectal forms, like "al-ra'fah" and "al-ra'afah."

It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with the extra letters dropped; the original is "al-inshā'ah."

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾, meaning: after the final creation He punishes whom He wills to punish, namely the disbelievers and the disobedient, and has mercy on whom He wills, namely the believers in Him, who confirm His messengers and act upon His commands and prohibitions. ﴿And to Him you will be turned﴾, meaning: you will be returned and brought back, not to any other.

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] in the earth or in the heaven﴾. al-Farra' said: "Nor those in the heaven can escape Allah in it," and he said: it is like the saying of Hassan:
"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises and supports him, are equal."
meaning: whoever praises and supports him is equal.

Similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: none but one who has a known station. The meaning is that neither the people of the earth nor the people of the heaven can overpower Him, glory be to Him, in the heaven, should they disobey Him.

Qutrub said: the meaning of the verse is: "nor in the heaven, even if you were in it," as you say: "So-and-so will not escape me here, nor in Basra," meaning: nor in Basra even if he went there.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "nor those in the heaven," with "man" not being a relative pronoun but an indefinite, and "in the heaven" being an adjective of it; the adjective is placed in the position of the noun modified. 'Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this and said: it is not permissible, and he preferred what Qutrub said.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, where "min" is extra for emphasis, meaning: you have no protector who will befriend you, nor a helper who will support you and repel from you the punishment of Allah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and His meeting﴾. The "signs" are either the revealed signs, the cosmic signs, or both. "Disbelieved in the meeting of Allah" means: they denied the resurrection and what follows it, and did not act upon what the messengers of Allah, glory be to Him, informed them of. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers to the disbelievers in the signs and the meeting; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they have despaired of My mercy﴾, meaning: they are in this world hopeless of Allah's mercy; what was revealed in the books of Allah and what His messengers told them did not benefit them.

It has also been said: the meaning is that they will despair on the Day of Resurrection of Allah's mercy, which is Paradise.

The meaning is that they despaired of mercy. ﴿And those will have a painful punishment﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the demonstrative for emphasis, and described the punishment as painful to indicate that it is at the extreme of severity.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him."﴾ This is a return to address Abraham after the interjection of what preceded, of address to Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the view of one who says that His saying "Say, travel through the earth" is address to Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the view that it is address to Abraham (peace be upon him), then the discourse in its context before and after is about Abraham, meaning: some of them said to others during their consultation: "Do to Abraham one of the two matters mentioned," and then they agreed upon burning him. ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ He made it cool and safe for him. Indeed in that, that is, in Allah's saving Abraham, are clear signs, meaning: manifest proofs and evident marks of the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His making: where they kindled that great fire and threw him into it, yet it did not burn him nor affect him at all, but rather it turned into a state contrary to what is its nature of heat and burning. The believers were specifically mentioned because they are the ones who take heed by the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, while others are heedless of that.

Al-Jumhur read "jawaba qawmihi" in the accusative, as the predicate of "kana," with what follows as its subject. Salim al-Aftas, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-Hasan read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with what follows in an accusative position as the predicate.

﴿And he said, "You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection between you in the worldly life"﴾, meaning: Abraham said to his people: for mutual affection among you and connection through your unity in worshipping them, and out of fear that affection among you would vanish if you abandon their worship.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "mawaddata baynikum," with the nominative "mawaddatu" without tanwin and idafah to "baynikum."

al-A'mash and Ibn Thabbit read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and tanwin.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "mawaddatan" with the accusative and tanwin, and read "baynakum" as an adverbial of place.

Hamzah and Hafs read "mawaddata" with the accusative, in idafah to "baynikum."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 2 of 2):

As for the reading with *raf'* (nominative, *raf'* meaning the nominative case), al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) mentioned two aspects for it. The first is that it is in the predicate of *inna* in *innama attakhadhtum*, and he took *ma* to be descriptive (*mawsufa*). The meaning is: "Indeed, that which you have taken besides Allah as idols is the affection among you."

The second aspect is that it is in the nominative by the omission of a subject, i.e., "it is affection," or "that is affection."

The meaning is that affection is what brought you together in worshipping and taking idols.

It has been said that *mawaddatu* may also be in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being *fi al-hayat al-dunya* ("in the life of this world").

As for the one who read *mawaddatan* with *raf'* and with *tanwin* (nunation), its explanation is like the first reading, with *baynikum* in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarfiyya*).

As for the one who read *mawaddata* with *nasb* (accusative) without *tanwin*, he made it the object of *attakhadhtum*, and he made *innama* a single particle of restriction (*li al-hasr*). The same applies to the one who read it with accusative and *tanwin*.

It is possible that the accusative in these two readings is because affection is the cause, so it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). In the reading with *raf'*, the second object of *attakhadhtum* is omitted, meaning "idols, gods." And on the assumption that *ma* in His saying *innama attakhadhtum* is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), the first object is its pronoun, i.e., *attakhadhtumuhu* ("you took it"), and the second object is *awthanan* ("idols").

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others﴾, i.e., some of those who took idols and worshipped them will disavow the others among them. So the leaders will disown the followers, and the followers will disown the leaders. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who worship idols will disown the idols, and the idols will disown those who worship them.

﴿And some of you will curse others﴾, i.e., each group will curse the other, according to the two explanations mentioned. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾, i.e., the disbelievers. It has been said that the idols are included in this, meaning the Fire is your dwelling place to which you return. ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who could rescue you from it by their help to you.

﴿So Lot believed him﴾, i.e., Lot believed in Abraham, and confirmed him in all that he brought. It has been said that he did not believe in him until he saw that the fire did not burn him. Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord"﴾. Al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: the one who said "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord" is Abraham.

Qatadah said: He emigrated from Kuthaa, which is a village in the region of Kufa, to Harran, then to Syria, and with him were his nephew Lot and his wife Sarah. The meaning is: "Indeed I am emigrating from the land of my people to where I may worship my Lord." ﴿Indeed He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the Mighty, whose actions proceed according to the requirements of wisdom.

It has been said that the speaker of ﴿Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord﴾ is Lot. But the first is preferable, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ refers to Abraham, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. All these pronouns refer to Abraham without any disagreement. The meaning is that Allah bestowed children upon him: He gave him Isaac as a son to him, and Jacob as a son to his son Isaac, and placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book. So Allah did not send a prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. The word *al-Kitab* (the Book) is singular because the definite article *al-* in it is for the genus, which includes all Books, and what is meant are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ is that he was given children in this world, and Allah informed him that prophethood would continue among them, and that is among the things that comfort his eye and increase his joy. It has also been said that his reward in this world is that the people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them.

It has been said that He gave him in this world good deeds and a good end. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, i.e., among those perfected in righteousness, deserving of full reward and abundant gifts from the Lord, glory be to Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah sent Noah when he was forty years old, and he remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah. He lived after the Flood sixty years until people multiplied and spread.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Noah's age before he was sent to his people and after he was sent was one thousand seven hundred years.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Awf ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Indeed Allah sent Noah to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years. Then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book *Dhamm al-Dunya* (Censure of the World) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasures?" He said: "Like a man who entered a house with two doors, stood in the middle of the house for a little while, then left through the other door."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾, that he said: Allah preserved it as a sign, and it is on al-Judi (a mountain).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And you invent a lie﴾, that he said: "You say falsehood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "the final creation," that he said: It is life after death, which is the resurrection.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that he said: "Lot confirmed Abraham."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The first of the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia with his family was Uthman ibn Affan. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah accompany them both. Indeed Uthman is the first to emigrate to Allah with his family after Lot.'"

Ibn Mandah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Uthman emigrated to Abyssinia, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed he is the first to emigrate after Abraham and Lot.'"

Ibn Asakir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim in *al-Kuna* narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between Uthman and Ruqayyah and Lot there was no emigrant."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The first to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Uthman ibn Affan, just as Lot emigrated to Abraham.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, that he said: "They were two sons of Abraham." And regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, he said: "Indeed Allah enjoined upon the people of the religions His religion, so there is no people of any religion but that they claim Abraham and are pleased with him."

These same narrators also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, that he said: "The good remembrance."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, saying: "The righteous child and good praise." As for Ibn Abbas's saying "they were two sons of Abraham," perhaps he means his son and his grandson, since a grandson is in the position of a son. Something like this would not be hidden from someone like Ibn Abbas, for he is the scholar (*hibr*) of this nation. This narration from him is from the narration of al-‘Awfi. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated: "Indeed the noble, son of a noble, son of a noble, son of a noble is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1116) Allah, glory be to Him, summarized the story of Noah as a confirmation of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We had certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]. In it is a strengthening (tathbit) for the Prophet (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, and none believed from among them except a few. So you are more worthy of patience, given the shortness of your period and the multitude of your community.

It has been said: The wording used is "a thousand years less fifty years" and not "nine hundred and fifty years," because the exception conveys precision in the number, unlike the latter, which may be used for what is approximate.

The amount of Noah's lifespan has been disputed, and this will come at the end of the discussion.

The verse says only that he remained among them this period, and it does not indicate that this was the whole of his life. He had already dwelt among others before dwelling among them, and he dwelt on the earth after their destruction by the flood. The fa' in ﴿So the flood seized them﴾ indicates sequence, meaning: it seized them immediately upon the completion of the stated period. The word "tufan" (flood) is used for anything abundant that encompasses a group and surrounds them, whether rain, killing, or death, as al-Nahhas said.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is rain. al-Dahhak said: drowning. It has also been said: death, and from it is the saying of the poet:
"Death's overwhelming flood destroyed them"

The clause ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they were persistent in wrongdoing, and what Noah admonished them with and reminded them of over this long period did not benefit them.

﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾, meaning: We saved Noah and We saved those who were with him in the ship from his children and followers.

The number of those people has been disputed, with several opinions. ﴿And We made it—i.e., the ship—a sign for the worlds﴾, meaning: a great lesson for them. Regarding its being a sign, there are several aspects: First, that it remained on al-Judi for a long time. Second, that Allah protected the ship from the violent winds. Third, that the water subsided before the provisions ran out.

This does not fit the description of the ship as a sign made by Allah. It has also been said that the pronoun in "made it" refers to the event, or to the deliverance, or to the punishment by drowning.

﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾: the accusative of Abraham is by coordination with Noah.

al-Nasa'i said: it is coordinated with the hā' in "made it" (ja'alnāhā). It has also been said: it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "And remember Abraham."

"When" (idh qāla) is accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: We sent Abraham at the time of his saying to his people, "Worship Allah," or: We made Abraham a sign at the time of this saying, or: remember Abraham at the time of his saying, the adverbial phrase being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for Abraham. ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾, meaning: single Him out for worship and devote worship to Him, and fear Him by not associating anything with Him. ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: the worship of Allah and fearing Him is better for you than associating partners with Him, and there is no good at all in shirk. But He addressed them in accordance with their belief: ﴿if you know﴾ anything of knowledge, or know knowledge by which you distinguish between what is good and what is evil.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-Ibrahim" with the accusative, and its explanation is as we mentioned.

al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far and Abu Hanifa read it with the nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is implied, meaning: and among the messengers is Abraham.

﴿You only worship idols besides Allah﴾: Abraham made clear to them that they worship what neither benefits nor harms, neither hears nor sees. The awthan (idols) are the asnam (images).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the sanam is what is made of gold, silver or copper, and the wathan is what is made of plaster or stone.

al-Jawhari said: the wathan is the sanam, and the plural is awthan. ﴿And you fabricate a falsehood﴾, meaning: you lie with a lie. This is on the understanding that takhluqun means "you lie." It may also mean: you make and carve them, i.e., you make them and carve them for falsehood.

al-Hasan said: the meaning of takhluqun is tanhitun (you carve), meaning: you worship idols while you make them.

Al-Jumhur read "takhluqun" with a fatha on the taa' (second person), a sukun on the khaa', and a damma on the lam, as the present tense of khalaqa; and "ifkan" with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the fa'.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Sulami and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the khaa' and the lam shaddah, the original being tatakhallaqun.

It is narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali that he read it with a damma on the taa' and a shaddah on the lam with a kasra.

Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Warqan read "afikan" with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like "al-kadhib" (lying), or an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a fabricated creation.

﴿Those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾, meaning: they are not able to provide you with any sustenance. ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾, meaning: direct your desire for your provision to Allah, for He is the one with whom all provision lies. So ask Him of His bounty, single Him out and do not single out others, and ﴿be grateful to Him﴾, meaning: for His blessings, for gratitude makes them lasting and is a cause for more of them. It is said: "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾, through death and then through resurrection, not to any other.

﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾. It has been said: this is from the words of Abraham, meaning: if you deny me, then this has happened to others before you. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him, meaning: if you deny Muhammad, then that is the custom of the disbelievers with those who came before. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ to his people to whom he was sent, and it is not incumbent upon him to guide them, nor is that within his capacity.

meaning: whoever praises and supports him is equal.

Indeed in that, that is, in Allah's saving Abraham, are clear signs, meaning: manifest proofs and evident marks of the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His making: where they kindled that great fire and threw him into it, yet it did not burn him nor affect him at all, but rather it turned into a state contrary to what is its nature of heat and burning. The believers were specifically mentioned because they are the ones who take heed by the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, while others are heedless of that.

Al-Jumhur read "jawaba qawmihi" in the accusative, as the predicate of "kana," with what follows as its subject. Salim al-Aftas, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-Hasan read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with what follows in an accusative position as the predicate.

﴿And he said, "You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection between you in the worldly life"﴾, meaning: Abraham said to his people: for mutual affection among you and connection through your unity in worshipping them, and out of fear that affection among you would vanish if you abandon their worship.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "mawaddata baynikum," with the nominative "mawaddatu" without tanwin and idafah to "baynikum."

al-A'mash and Ibn Thabbit read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and tanwin.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "mawaddatan" with the accusative and tanwin, and read "baynakum" as an adverbial of place.

Hamzah and Hafs read "mawaddata" with the accusative, in idafah to "baynikum."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 2 of 2):

As for the reading with *raf'* (nominative, *raf'* meaning the nominative case), al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) mentioned two aspects for it. The first is that it is in the predicate of *inna* in *innama attakhadhtum*, and he took *ma* to be descriptive (*mawsufa*). The meaning is: "Indeed, that which you have taken besides Allah as idols is the affection among you."

The second aspect is that it is in the nominative by the omission of a subject, i.e., "it is affection," or "that is affection."

The meaning is that affection is what brought you together in worshipping and taking idols.

It has been said that *mawaddatu* may also be in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being *fi al-hayat al-dunya* ("in the life of this world").

As for the one who read *mawaddatan* with *raf'* and with *tanwin* (nunation), its explanation is like the first reading, with *baynikum* in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarfiyya*).

As for the one who read *mawaddata* with *nasb* (accusative) without *tanwin*, he made it the object of *attakhadhtum*, and he made *innama* a single particle of restriction (*li al-hasr*). The same applies to the one who read it with accusative and *tanwin*.

It is possible that the accusative in these two readings is because affection is the cause, so it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). In the reading with *raf'*, the second object of *attakhadhtum* is omitted, meaning "idols, gods." And on the assumption that *ma* in His saying *innama attakhadhtum* is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), the first object is its pronoun, i.e., *attakhadhtumuhu* ("you took it"), and the second object is *awthanan* ("idols").

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others﴾, i.e., some of those who took idols and worshipped them will disavow the others among them. So the leaders will disown the followers, and the followers will disown the leaders. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who worship idols will disown the idols, and the idols will disown those who worship them.

﴿And some of you will curse others﴾, i.e., each group will curse the other, according to the two explanations mentioned. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾, i.e., the disbelievers. It has been said that the idols are included in this, meaning the Fire is your dwelling place to which you return. ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who could rescue you from it by their help to you.

﴿So Lot believed him﴾, i.e., Lot believed in Abraham, and confirmed him in all that he brought. It has been said that he did not believe in him until he saw that the fire did not burn him. Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord"﴾. Al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: the one who said "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord" is Abraham.

Qatadah said: He emigrated from Kuthaa, which is a village in the region of Kufa, to Harran, then to Syria, and with him were his nephew Lot and his wife Sarah. The meaning is: "Indeed I am emigrating from the land of my people to where I may worship my Lord." ﴿Indeed He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the Mighty, whose actions proceed according to the requirements of wisdom.

It has been said that the speaker of ﴿Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord﴾ is Lot. But the first is preferable, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ refers to Abraham, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. All these pronouns refer to Abraham without any disagreement. The meaning is that Allah bestowed children upon him: He gave him Isaac as a son to him, and Jacob as a son to his son Isaac, and placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book. So Allah did not send a prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. The word *al-Kitab* (the Book) is singular because the definite article *al-* in it is for the genus, which includes all Books, and what is meant are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ is that he was given children in this world, and Allah informed him that prophethood would continue among them, and that is among the things that comfort his eye and increase his joy. It has also been said that his reward in this world is that the people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them.

It has been said that He gave him in this world good deeds and a good end. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, i.e., among those perfected in righteousness, deserving of full reward and abundant gifts from the Lord, glory be to Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah sent Noah when he was forty years old, and he remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah. He lived after the Flood sixty years until people multiplied and spread.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Noah's age before he was sent to his people and after he was sent was one thousand seven hundred years.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Awf ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Indeed Allah sent Noah to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years. Then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book *Dhamm al-Dunya* (Censure of the World) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasures?" He said: "Like a man who entered a house with two doors, stood in the middle of the house for a little while, then left through the other door."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾, that he said: Allah preserved it as a sign, and it is on al-Judi (a mountain).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And you invent a lie﴾, that he said: "You say falsehood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "the final creation," that he said: It is life after death, which is the resurrection.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that he said: "Lot confirmed Abraham."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The first of the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia with his family was Uthman ibn Affan. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah accompany them both. Indeed Uthman is the first to emigrate to Allah with his family after Lot.'"

Ibn Mandah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Uthman emigrated to Abyssinia, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed he is the first to emigrate after Abraham and Lot.'"

Ibn Asakir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim in *al-Kuna* narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between Uthman and Ruqayyah and Lot there was no emigrant."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The first to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Uthman ibn Affan, just as Lot emigrated to Abraham.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, that he said: "They were two sons of Abraham." And regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, he said: "Indeed Allah enjoined upon the people of the religions His religion, so there is no people of any religion but that they claim Abraham and are pleased with him."

These same narrators also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, that he said: "The good remembrance."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, saying: "The righteous child and good praise." As for Ibn Abbas's saying "they were two sons of Abraham," perhaps he means his son and his grandson, since a grandson is in the position of a son. Something like this would not be hidden from someone like Ibn Abbas, for he is the scholar (*hibr*) of this nation. This narration from him is from the narration of al-‘Awfi. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated: "Indeed the noble, son of a noble, son of a noble, son of a noble is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1116) Allah, glory be to Him, summarized the story of Noah as a confirmation of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We had certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]. In it is a strengthening (tathbit) for the Prophet (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, and none believed from among them except a few. So you are more worthy of patience, given the shortness of your period and the multitude of your community.

It has been said: The wording used is "a thousand years less fifty years" and not "nine hundred and fifty years," because the exception conveys precision in the number, unlike the latter, which may be used for what is approximate.

The amount of Noah's lifespan has been disputed, and this will come at the end of the discussion.

The verse says only that he remained among them this period, and it does not indicate that this was the whole of his life. He had already dwelt among others before dwelling among them, and he dwelt on the earth after their destruction by the flood. The fa' in ﴿So the flood seized them﴾ indicates sequence, meaning: it seized them immediately upon the completion of the stated period. The word "tufan" (flood) is used for anything abundant that encompasses a group and surrounds them, whether rain, killing, or death, as al-Nahhas said.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is rain. al-Dahhak said: drowning. It has also been said: death, and from it is the saying of the poet:
"Death's overwhelming flood destroyed them"

The clause ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they were persistent in wrongdoing, and what Noah admonished them with and reminded them of over this long period did not benefit them.

﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾, meaning: We saved Noah and We saved those who were with him in the ship from his children and followers.

The number of those people has been disputed, with several opinions. ﴿And We made it—i.e., the ship—a sign for the worlds﴾, meaning: a great lesson for them. Regarding its being a sign, there are several aspects: First, that it remained on al-Judi for a long time. Second, that Allah protected the ship from the violent winds. Third, that the water subsided before the provisions ran out.

This does not fit the description of the ship as a sign made by Allah. It has also been said that the pronoun in "made it" refers to the event, or to the deliverance, or to the punishment by drowning.

﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾: the accusative of Abraham is by coordination with Noah.

al-Nasa'i said: it is coordinated with the hā' in "made it" (ja'alnāhā). It has also been said: it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "And remember Abraham."

"When" (idh qāla) is accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: We sent Abraham at the time of his saying to his people, "Worship Allah," or: We made Abraham a sign at the time of this saying, or: remember Abraham at the time of his saying, the adverbial phrase being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for Abraham. ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾, meaning: single Him out for worship and devote worship to Him, and fear Him by not associating anything with Him. ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: the worship of Allah and fearing Him is better for you than associating partners with Him, and there is no good at all in shirk. But He addressed them in accordance with their belief: ﴿if you know﴾ anything of knowledge, or know knowledge by which you distinguish between what is good and what is evil.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-Ibrahim" with the accusative, and its explanation is as we mentioned.

al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far and Abu Hanifa read it with the nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is implied, meaning: and among the messengers is Abraham.

﴿You only worship idols besides Allah﴾: Abraham made clear to them that they worship what neither benefits nor harms, neither hears nor sees. The awthan (idols) are the asnam (images).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the sanam is what is made of gold, silver or copper, and the wathan is what is made of plaster or stone.

al-Jawhari said: the wathan is the sanam, and the plural is awthan. ﴿And you fabricate a falsehood﴾, meaning: you lie with a lie. This is on the understanding that takhluqun means "you lie." It may also mean: you make and carve them, i.e., you make them and carve them for falsehood.

al-Hasan said: the meaning of takhluqun is tanhitun (you carve), meaning: you worship idols while you make them.

Al-Jumhur read "takhluqun" with a fatha on the taa' (second person), a sukun on the khaa', and a damma on the lam, as the present tense of khalaqa; and "ifkan" with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the fa'.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Sulami and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the khaa' and the lam shaddah, the original being tatakhallaqun.

It is narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali that he read it with a damma on the taa' and a shaddah on the lam with a kasra.

Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Warqan read "afikan" with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like "al-kadhib" (lying), or an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a fabricated creation.

﴿Those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾, meaning: they are not able to provide you with any sustenance. ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾, meaning: direct your desire for your provision to Allah, for He is the one with whom all provision lies. So ask Him of His bounty, single Him out and do not single out others, and ﴿be grateful to Him﴾, meaning: for His blessings, for gratitude makes them lasting and is a cause for more of them. It is said: "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾, through death and then through resurrection, not to any other.

﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾. It has been said: this is from the words of Abraham, meaning: if you deny me, then this has happened to others before you. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him, meaning: if you deny Muhammad, then that is the custom of the disbelievers with those who came before. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ to his people to whom he was sent, and it is not incumbent upon him to guide them, nor is that within his capacity.

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ Al-Jumhur read "awa-lam yaraw" with the yā' (third person), as a report; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is as if he said: "Have the nations not seen?"

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbit, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the tā' (second person) as an address from Abraham to his people. It has also been said that it is an address from Allah to the Quraysh.

Al-Jumhur read "kayfa yubdi'" with a damma on the yā', from abda'a yubdi'u. Al-Zubayri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha, from bada'a yabda'u.

al-Zuhri read "kayfa bada'a," and the meaning is: have they not seen how Allah creates them originally, a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then breathes the spirit into it, then brings it out into the world, then causes it to die afterward? Likewise all animals and all plants. So when you see Allah's power over origination and bringing into being, He is the one able to repeat it. The hamza is for denying that they have not seen, and the waw is for coordination with an implied clause. ﴿Indeed that, for Allah, is easy﴾, because when He wills a matter, He says to it "Be," and it is.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded Abraham to tell his people to travel in the land, (p-1117) so that they might reflect and take heed. He said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation"﴾, with their multitude, diversity of colors, natures and languages. And look at the dwelling places of the past generations and the extinct nations and their remains, so that by this you may know the perfection of Allah's power.

It has also been said that the meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, "Travel." The meaning of His saying ﴿Then Allah produces the final creation﴾ is that Allah who began the first creation and created it in that manner will produce it a second time at the resurrection. The clause is coordinated with the clause "travel through the earth," and both are within the scope of "say." The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read "al-nash'ah" with a short vowel and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a long vowel and a fatha on the shin; both are dialectal forms, like "al-ra'fah" and "al-ra'afah."

It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with the extra letters dropped; the original is "al-inshā'ah."

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾, meaning: after the final creation He punishes whom He wills to punish, namely the disbelievers and the disobedient, and has mercy on whom He wills, namely the believers in Him, who confirm His messengers and act upon His commands and prohibitions. ﴿And to Him you will be turned﴾, meaning: you will be returned and brought back, not to any other.

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] in the earth or in the heaven﴾. al-Farra' said: "Nor those in the heaven can escape Allah in it," and he said: it is like the saying of Hassan:
"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises and supports him, are equal."
meaning: whoever praises and supports him is equal.

Similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: none but one who has a known station. The meaning is that neither the people of the earth nor the people of the heaven can overpower Him, glory be to Him, in the heaven, should they disobey Him.

Qutrub said: the meaning of the verse is: "nor in the heaven, even if you were in it," as you say: "So-and-so will not escape me here, nor in Basra," meaning: nor in Basra even if he went there.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "nor those in the heaven," with "man" not being a relative pronoun but an indefinite, and "in the heaven" being an adjective of it; the adjective is placed in the position of the noun modified. 'Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this and said: it is not permissible, and he preferred what Qutrub said.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, where "min" is extra for emphasis, meaning: you have no protector who will befriend you, nor a helper who will support you and repel from you the punishment of Allah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and His meeting﴾. The "signs" are either the revealed signs, the cosmic signs, or both. "Disbelieved in the meeting of Allah" means: they denied the resurrection and what follows it, and did not act upon what the messengers of Allah, glory be to Him, informed them of. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers to the disbelievers in the signs and the meeting; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they have despaired of My mercy﴾, meaning: they are in this world hopeless of Allah's mercy; what was revealed in the books of Allah and what His messengers told them did not benefit them.

It has also been said: the meaning is that they will despair on the Day of Resurrection of Allah's mercy, which is Paradise.

The meaning is that they despaired of mercy. ﴿And those will have a painful punishment﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the demonstrative for emphasis, and described the punishment as painful to indicate that it is at the extreme of severity.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him."﴾ This is a return to address Abraham after the interjection of what preceded, of address to Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the view of one who says that His saying "Say, travel through the earth" is address to Muhammad (ﷺ). The word *al-Kitab* (the Book) is singular because the definite article *al-* in it is for the genus, which includes all Books, and what is meant are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ is that he was given children in this world, and Allah informed him that prophethood would continue among them, and that is among the things that comfort his eye and increase his joy. It has also been said that his reward in this world is that the people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them.

It has been said that He gave him in this world good deeds and a good end. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, i.e., among those perfected in righteousness, deserving of full reward and abundant gifts from the Lord, glory be to Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah sent Noah when he was forty years old, and he remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah. He lived after the Flood sixty years until people multiplied and spread.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Noah's age before he was sent to his people and after he was sent was one thousand seven hundred years.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Awf ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Indeed Allah sent Noah to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years. Then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book *Dhamm al-Dunya* (Censure of the World) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasures?" He said: "Like a man who entered a house with two doors, stood in the middle of the house for a little while, then left through the other door."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾, that he said: Allah preserved it as a sign, and it is on al-Judi (a mountain).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And you invent a lie﴾, that he said: "You say falsehood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "the final creation," that he said: It is life after death, which is the resurrection.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that he said: "Lot confirmed Abraham."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The first of the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia with his family was Uthman ibn Affan. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah accompany them both. Indeed Uthman is the first to emigrate to Allah with his family after Lot.'"

Ibn Mandah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Uthman emigrated to Abyssinia, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed he is the first to emigrate after Abraham and Lot.'"

Ibn Asakir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim in *al-Kuna* narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between Uthman and Ruqayyah and Lot there was no emigrant."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The first to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Uthman ibn Affan, just as Lot emigrated to Abraham.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, that he said: "They were two sons of Abraham." And regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, he said: "Indeed Allah enjoined upon the people of the religions His religion, so there is no people of any religion but that they claim Abraham and are pleased with him."

These same narrators also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, that he said: "The good remembrance."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, saying: "The righteous child and good praise." As for Ibn Abbas's saying "they were two sons of Abraham," perhaps he means his son and his grandson, since a grandson is in the position of a son. Something like this would not be hidden from someone like Ibn Abbas, for he is the scholar (*hibr*) of this nation. This narration from him is from the narration of al-‘Awfi. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated: "Indeed the noble, son of a noble, son of a noble, son of a noble is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1116) Allah, glory be to Him, summarized the story of Noah as a confirmation of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We had certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]. In it is a strengthening (tathbit) for the Prophet (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, and none believed from among them except a few. So you are more worthy of patience, given the shortness of your period and the multitude of your community.

It has been said: The wording used is "a thousand years less fifty years" and not "nine hundred and fifty years," because the exception conveys precision in the number, unlike the latter, which may be used for what is approximate.

The amount of Noah's lifespan has been disputed, and this will come at the end of the discussion.

The verse says only that he remained among them this period, and it does not indicate that this was the whole of his life. He had already dwelt among others before dwelling among them, and he dwelt on the earth after their destruction by the flood. The fa' in ﴿So the flood seized them﴾ indicates sequence, meaning: it seized them immediately upon the completion of the stated period. The word "tufan" (flood) is used for anything abundant that encompasses a group and surrounds them, whether rain, killing, or death, as al-Nahhas said.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is rain. al-Dahhak said: drowning. It has also been said: death, and from it is the saying of the poet:
"Death's overwhelming flood destroyed them"

The clause ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they were persistent in wrongdoing, and what Noah admonished them with and reminded them of over this long period did not benefit them.

﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾, meaning: We saved Noah and We saved those who were with him in the ship from his children and followers.

The number of those people has been disputed, with several opinions. ﴿And We made it—i.e., the ship—a sign for the worlds﴾, meaning: a great lesson for them. Regarding its being a sign, there are several aspects: First, that it remained on al-Judi for a long time. Second, that Allah protected the ship from the violent winds. Third, that the water subsided before the provisions ran out.

This does not fit the description of the ship as a sign made by Allah. It has also been said that the pronoun in "made it" refers to the event, or to the deliverance, or to the punishment by drowning.

﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾: the accusative of Abraham is by coordination with Noah.

al-Nasa'i said: it is coordinated with the hā' in "made it" (ja'alnāhā). It has also been said: it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "And remember Abraham."

"When" (idh qāla) is accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: We sent Abraham at the time of his saying to his people, "Worship Allah," or: We made Abraham a sign at the time of this saying, or: remember Abraham at the time of his saying, the adverbial phrase being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for Abraham. ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾, meaning: single Him out for worship and devote worship to Him, and fear Him by not associating anything with Him. ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: the worship of Allah and fearing Him is better for you than associating partners with Him, and there is no good at all in shirk. But He addressed them in accordance with their belief: ﴿if you know﴾ anything of knowledge, or know knowledge by which you distinguish between what is good and what is evil.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-Ibrahim" with the accusative, and its explanation is as we mentioned.

al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far and Abu Hanifa read it with the nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is implied, meaning: and among the messengers is Abraham.

﴿You only worship idols besides Allah﴾: Abraham made clear to them that they worship what neither benefits nor harms, neither hears nor sees. The awthan (idols) are the asnam (images).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the sanam is what is made of gold, silver or copper, and the wathan is what is made of plaster or stone.

al-Jawhari said: the wathan is the sanam, and the plural is awthan. ﴿And you fabricate a falsehood﴾, meaning: you lie with a lie. This is on the understanding that takhluqun means "you lie." It may also mean: you make and carve them, i.e., you make them and carve them for falsehood.

al-Hasan said: the meaning of takhluqun is tanhitun (you carve), meaning: you worship idols while you make them.

Al-Jumhur read "takhluqun" with a fatha on the taa' (second person), a sukun on the khaa', and a damma on the lam, as the present tense of khalaqa; and "ifkan" with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the fa'.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Sulami and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the khaa' and the lam shaddah, the original being tatakhallaqun.

It is narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali that he read it with a damma on the taa' and a shaddah on the lam with a kasra.

Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Warqan read "afikan" with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like "al-kadhib" (lying), or an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a fabricated creation.

﴿Those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾, meaning: they are not able to provide you with any sustenance. ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾, meaning: direct your desire for your provision to Allah, for He is the one with whom all provision lies. So ask Him of His bounty, single Him out and do not single out others, and ﴿be grateful to Him﴾, meaning: for His blessings, for gratitude makes them lasting and is a cause for more of them. It is said: "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾, through death and then through resurrection, not to any other.

﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾. It has been said: this is from the words of Abraham, meaning: if you deny me, then this has happened to others before you. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him, meaning: if you deny Muhammad, then that is the custom of the disbelievers with those who came before. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ to his people to whom he was sent, and it is not incumbent upon him to guide them, nor is that within his capacity.

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ Al-Jumhur read "awa-lam yaraw" with the yā' (third person), as a report; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is as if he said: "Have the nations not seen?"

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbit, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the tā' (second person) as an address from Abraham to his people. It has also been said that it is an address from Allah to the Quraysh.

Al-Jumhur read "kayfa yubdi'" with a damma on the yā', from abda'a yubdi'u. Al-Zubayri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha, from bada'a yabda'u.

al-Zuhri read "kayfa bada'a," and the meaning is: have they not seen how Allah creates them originally, a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then breathes the spirit into it, then brings it out into the world, then causes it to die afterward? Likewise all animals and all plants. So when you see Allah's power over origination and bringing into being, He is the one able to repeat it. The hamza is for denying that they have not seen, and the waw is for coordination with an implied clause. ﴿Indeed that, for Allah, is easy﴾, because when He wills a matter, He says to it "Be," and it is.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded Abraham to tell his people to travel in the land, (p-1117) so that they might reflect and take heed. He said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation"﴾, with their multitude, diversity of colors, natures and languages. And look at the dwelling places of the past generations and the extinct nations and their remains, so that by this you may know the perfection of Allah's power.

It has also been said that the meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, "Travel." The meaning of His saying ﴿Then Allah produces the final creation﴾ is that Allah who began the first creation and created it in that manner will produce it a second time at the resurrection. The clause is coordinated with the clause "travel through the earth," and both are within the scope of "say." The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read "al-nash'ah" with a short vowel and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a long vowel and a fatha on the shin; both are dialectal forms, like "al-ra'fah" and "al-ra'afah."

It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with the extra letters dropped; the original is "al-inshā'ah."

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾, meaning: after the final creation He punishes whom He wills to punish, namely the disbelievers and the disobedient, and has mercy on whom He wills, namely the believers in Him, who confirm His messengers and act upon His commands and prohibitions. ﴿And to Him you will be turned﴾, meaning: you will be returned and brought back, not to any other.

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] in the earth or in the heaven﴾. al-Farra' said: "Nor those in the heaven can escape Allah in it," and he said: it is like the saying of Hassan:
"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises and supports him, are equal."
meaning: whoever praises and supports him is equal.

Similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: none but one who has a known station. The meaning is that neither the people of the earth nor the people of the heaven can overpower Him, glory be to Him, in the heaven, should they disobey Him.

Qutrub said: the meaning of the verse is: "nor in the heaven, even if you were in it," as you say: "So-and-so will not escape me here, nor in Basra," meaning: nor in Basra even if he went there.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "nor those in the heaven," with "man" not being a relative pronoun but an indefinite, and "in the heaven" being an adjective of it; the adjective is placed in the position of the noun modified. 'Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this and said: it is not permissible, and he preferred what Qutrub said.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, where "min" is extra for emphasis, meaning: you have no protector who will befriend you, nor a helper who will support you and repel from you the punishment of Allah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and His meeting﴾. The "signs" are either the revealed signs, the cosmic signs, or both. "Disbelieved in the meeting of Allah" means: they denied the resurrection and what follows it, and did not act upon what the messengers of Allah, glory be to Him, informed them of. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers to the disbelievers in the signs and the meeting; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they have despaired of My mercy﴾, meaning: they are in this world hopeless of Allah's mercy; what was revealed in the books of Allah and what His messengers told them did not benefit them.

It has also been said: the meaning is that they will despair on the Day of Resurrection of Allah's mercy, which is Paradise.

The meaning is that they despaired of mercy. ﴿And those will have a painful punishment﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the demonstrative for emphasis, and described the punishment as painful to indicate that it is at the extreme of severity.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him."﴾ This is a return to address Abraham after the interjection of what preceded, of address to Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the view of one who says that His saying "Say, travel through the earth" is address to Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the view that it is address to Abraham (peace be upon him), then the discourse in its context before and after is about Abraham, meaning: some of them said to others during their consultation: "Do to Abraham one of the two matters mentioned," and then they agreed upon burning him. ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ He made it cool and safe for him. Indeed in that, that is, in Allah's saving Abraham, are clear signs, meaning: manifest proofs and evident marks of the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His making: where they kindled that great fire and threw him into it, yet it did not burn him nor affect him at all, but rather it turned into a state contrary to what is its nature of heat and burning. The believers were specifically mentioned because they are the ones who take heed by the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, while others are heedless of that.

Al-Jumhur read "jawaba qawmihi" in the accusative, as the predicate of "kana," with what follows as its subject. Salim al-Aftas, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-Hasan read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with what follows in an accusative position as the predicate.

﴿And he said, "You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection between you in the worldly life"﴾, meaning: Abraham said to his people: for mutual affection among you and connection through your unity in worshipping them, and out of fear that affection among you would vanish if you abandon their worship.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "mawaddata baynikum," with the nominative "mawaddatu" without tanwin and idafah to "baynikum."

al-A'mash and Ibn Thabbit read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and tanwin.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "mawaddatan" with the accusative and tanwin, and read "baynakum" as an adverbial of place.

Hamzah and Hafs read "mawaddata" with the accusative, in idafah to "baynikum."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 2 of 2):

As for the reading with *raf'* (nominative, *raf'* meaning the nominative case), al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) mentioned two aspects for it. The first is that it is in the predicate of *inna* in *innama attakhadhtum*, and he took *ma* to be descriptive (*mawsufa*). The meaning is: "Indeed, that which you have taken besides Allah as idols is the affection among you."

The second aspect is that it is in the nominative by the omission of a subject, i.e., "it is affection," or "that is affection."

The meaning is that affection is what brought you together in worshipping and taking idols.

It has been said that *mawaddatu* may also be in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being *fi al-hayat al-dunya* ("in the life of this world").

As for the one who read *mawaddatan* with *raf'* and with *tanwin* (nunation), its explanation is like the first reading, with *baynikum* in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarfiyya*).

As for the one who read *mawaddata* with *nasb* (accusative) without *tanwin*, he made it the object of *attakhadhtum*, and he made *innama* a single particle of restriction (*li al-hasr*). The same applies to the one who read it with accusative and *tanwin*.

It is possible that the accusative in these two readings is because affection is the cause, so it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). In the reading with *raf'*, the second object of *attakhadhtum* is omitted, meaning "idols, gods." And on the assumption that *ma* in His saying *innama attakhadhtum* is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), the first object is its pronoun, i.e., *attakhadhtumuhu* ("you took it"), and the second object is *awthanan* ("idols").

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others﴾, i.e., some of those who took idols and worshipped them will disavow the others among them. So the leaders will disown the followers, and the followers will disown the leaders. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who worship idols will disown the idols, and the idols will disown those who worship them.

﴿And some of you will curse others﴾, i.e., each group will curse the other, according to the two explanations mentioned. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾, i.e., the disbelievers. It has been said that the idols are included in this, meaning the Fire is your dwelling place to which you return. ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who could rescue you from it by their help to you.

﴿So Lot believed him﴾, i.e., Lot believed in Abraham, and confirmed him in all that he brought. It has been said that he did not believe in him until he saw that the fire did not burn him. Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord"﴾. Al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: the one who said "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord" is Abraham.

Qatadah said: He emigrated from Kuthaa, which is a village in the region of Kufa, to Harran, then to Syria, and with him were his nephew Lot and his wife Sarah. The meaning is: "Indeed I am emigrating from the land of my people to where I may worship my Lord." ﴿Indeed He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the Mighty, whose actions proceed according to the requirements of wisdom.

It has been said that the speaker of ﴿Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord﴾ is Lot. But the first is preferable, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ refers to Abraham, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. All these pronouns refer to Abraham without any disagreement. The meaning is that Allah bestowed children upon him: He gave him Isaac as a son to him, and Jacob as a son to his son Isaac, and placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book. So Allah did not send a prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. The word *al-Kitab* (the Book) is singular because the definite article *al-* in it is for the genus, which includes all Books, and what is meant are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ is that he was given children in this world, and Allah informed him that prophethood would continue among them, and that is among the things that comfort his eye and increase his joy. It has also been said that his reward in this world is that the people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them.

It has been said that He gave him in this world good deeds and a good end. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, i.e., among those perfected in righteousness, deserving of full reward and abundant gifts from the Lord, glory be to Him.
