Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah sent Noah when he was forty years old, and he remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah. He lived after the Flood sixty years until people multiplied and spread.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Noah's age before he was sent to his people and after he was sent was one thousand seven hundred years.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Awf ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Indeed Allah sent Noah to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years. Then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book *Dhamm al-Dunya* (Censure of the World) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasures?" He said: "Like a man who entered a house with two doors, stood in the middle of the house for a little while, then left through the other door."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾, that he said: Allah preserved it as a sign, and it is on al-Judi (a mountain).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And you invent a lie﴾, that he said: "You say falsehood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "the final creation," that he said: It is life after death, which is the resurrection.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that he said: "Lot confirmed Abraham."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The first of the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia with his family was Uthman ibn Affan. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah accompany them both. Indeed Uthman is the first to emigrate to Allah with his family after Lot.'"

Ibn Mandah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Uthman emigrated to Abyssinia, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed he is the first to emigrate after Abraham and Lot.'"

Ibn Asakir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim in *al-Kuna* narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between Uthman and Ruqayyah and Lot there was no emigrant."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The first to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Uthman ibn Affan, just as Lot emigrated to Abraham.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, that he said: "They were two sons of Abraham." And regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, he said: "Indeed Allah enjoined upon the people of the religions His religion, so there is no people of any religion but that they claim Abraham and are pleased with him."

These same narrators also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, that he said: "The good remembrance."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, saying: "The righteous child and good praise." As for Ibn Abbas's saying "they were two sons of Abraham," perhaps he means his son and his grandson, since a grandson is in the position of a son. Something like this would not be hidden from someone like Ibn Abbas, for he is the scholar (*hibr*) of this nation. This narration from him is from the narration of al-‘Awfi. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated: "Indeed the noble, son of a noble, son of a noble, son of a noble is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1116) Allah, glory be to Him, summarized the story of Noah as a confirmation of His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿And We had certainly tested those before them﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3]. In it is a strengthening (tathbit) for the Prophet (ﷺ), as if it were said to him: Noah remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them, and none believed from among them except a few. So you are more worthy of patience, given the shortness of your period and the multitude of your community.

It has been said: The wording used is "a thousand years less fifty years" and not "nine hundred and fifty years," because the exception conveys precision in the number, unlike the latter, which may be used for what is approximate.

The amount of Noah's lifespan has been disputed, and this will come at the end of the discussion.

The verse says only that he remained among them this period, and it does not indicate that this was the whole of his life. He had already dwelt among others before dwelling among them, and he dwelt on the earth after their destruction by the flood. The fa' in ﴿So the flood seized them﴾ indicates sequence, meaning: it seized them immediately upon the completion of the stated period. The word "tufan" (flood) is used for anything abundant that encompasses a group and surrounds them, whether rain, killing, or death, as al-Nahhas said.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: it is rain. al-Dahhak said: drowning. It has also been said: death, and from it is the saying of the poet:
"Death's overwhelming flood destroyed them"

The clause ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they were persistent in wrongdoing, and what Noah admonished them with and reminded them of over this long period did not benefit them.

﴿So We saved him and the companions of the ship﴾, meaning: We saved Noah and We saved those who were with him in the ship from his children and followers.

The number of those people has been disputed, with several opinions. ﴿And We made it—i.e., the ship—a sign for the worlds﴾, meaning: a great lesson for them. Regarding its being a sign, there are several aspects: First, that it remained on al-Judi for a long time. Second, that Allah protected the ship from the violent winds. Third, that the water subsided before the provisions ran out.

This does not fit the description of the ship as a sign made by Allah. It has also been said that the pronoun in "made it" refers to the event, or to the deliverance, or to the punishment by drowning.

﴿And Abraham, when he said to his people﴾: the accusative of Abraham is by coordination with Noah.

al-Nasa'i said: it is coordinated with the hā' in "made it" (ja'alnāhā). It has also been said: it is accusative by an implied verb, meaning: "And remember Abraham."

"When" (idh qāla) is accusative as an adverb of time, meaning: We sent Abraham at the time of his saying to his people, "Worship Allah," or: We made Abraham a sign at the time of this saying, or: remember Abraham at the time of his saying, the adverbial phrase being a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for Abraham. ﴿Worship Allah and fear Him﴾, meaning: single Him out for worship and devote worship to Him, and fear Him by not associating anything with Him. ﴿That is better for you﴾, meaning: the worship of Allah and fearing Him is better for you than associating partners with Him, and there is no good at all in shirk. But He addressed them in accordance with their belief: ﴿if you know﴾ anything of knowledge, or know knowledge by which you distinguish between what is good and what is evil.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-Ibrahim" with the accusative, and its explanation is as we mentioned.

al-Nakha'i, Abu Ja'far and Abu Hanifa read it with the nominative, as an inchoative, and the predicate is implied, meaning: and among the messengers is Abraham.

﴿You only worship idols besides Allah﴾: Abraham made clear to them that they worship what neither benefits nor harms, neither hears nor sees. The awthan (idols) are the asnam (images).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: the sanam is what is made of gold, silver or copper, and the wathan is what is made of plaster or stone.

al-Jawhari said: the wathan is the sanam, and the plural is awthan. ﴿And you fabricate a falsehood﴾, meaning: you lie with a lie. This is on the understanding that takhluqun means "you lie." It may also mean: you make and carve them, i.e., you make them and carve them for falsehood.

al-Hasan said: the meaning of takhluqun is tanhitun (you carve), meaning: you worship idols while you make them.

Al-Jumhur read "takhluqun" with a fatha on the taa' (second person), a sukun on the khaa', and a damma on the lam, as the present tense of khalaqa; and "ifkan" with a kasra on the hamza and a sukun on the fa'.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn 'Ali, al-Sulami and Qatadah read it with a fatha on the khaa' and the lam shaddah, the original being tatakhallaqun.

It is narrated from Zayd ibn 'Ali that he read it with a damma on the taa' and a shaddah on the lam with a kasra.

Ibn al-Zubayr and Fudayl ibn Warqan read "afikan" with a fatha on the hamza and a kasra on the fa', and it is a verbal noun like "al-kadhib" (lying), or an adjective of an implied verbal noun, meaning: a fabricated creation.

﴿Those you worship besides Allah do not possess for you any provision﴾, meaning: they are not able to provide you with any sustenance. ﴿So seek provision from Allah﴾, meaning: direct your desire for your provision to Allah, for He is the one with whom all provision lies. So ask Him of His bounty, single Him out and do not single out others, and ﴿be grateful to Him﴾, meaning: for His blessings, for gratitude makes them lasting and is a cause for more of them. It is said: "shakartuhu" and "shakartu lahu." ﴿To Him you will be returned﴾, through death and then through resurrection, not to any other.

﴿And if you deny, then nations before you have denied﴾. It has been said: this is from the words of Abraham, meaning: if you deny me, then this has happened to others before you. It has also been said: this is from the words of Allah, glory be to Him, meaning: if you deny Muhammad, then that is the custom of the disbelievers with those who came before. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear notification﴾ to his people to whom he was sent, and it is not incumbent upon him to guide them, nor is that within his capacity.

﴿Have they not seen how Allah originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ Al-Jumhur read "awa-lam yaraw" with the yā' (third person), as a report; Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim chose this reading. Abu 'Ubayd said: it is as if he said: "Have the nations not seen?"

Abu Bakr, al-A'mash, Ibn Thabbit, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the tā' (second person) as an address from Abraham to his people. It has also been said that it is an address from Allah to the Quraysh.

Al-Jumhur read "kayfa yubdi'" with a damma on the yā', from abda'a yubdi'u. Al-Zubayri, 'Isa ibn 'Umar and Abu 'Amr read it with a fatha, from bada'a yabda'u.

al-Zuhri read "kayfa bada'a," and the meaning is: have they not seen how Allah creates them originally, a drop of semen, then a clinging clot, then a lump of flesh, then breathes the spirit into it, then brings it out into the world, then causes it to die afterward? Likewise all animals and all plants. So when you see Allah's power over origination and bringing into being, He is the one able to repeat it. The hamza is for denying that they have not seen, and the waw is for coordination with an implied clause. ﴿Indeed that, for Allah, is easy﴾, because when He wills a matter, He says to it "Be," and it is.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, commanded Abraham to tell his people to travel in the land, (p-1117) so that they might reflect and take heed. He said: ﴿Say, "Travel through the earth and observe how He began creation"﴾, with their multitude, diversity of colors, natures and languages. And look at the dwelling places of the past generations and the extinct nations and their remains, so that by this you may know the perfection of Allah's power.

It has also been said that the meaning is: say to them, O Muhammad, "Travel." The meaning of His saying ﴿Then Allah produces the final creation﴾ is that Allah who began the first creation and created it in that manner will produce it a second time at the resurrection. The clause is coordinated with the clause "travel through the earth," and both are within the scope of "say." The clause ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent﴾ is an explanation of what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read "al-nash'ah" with a short vowel and a sukun on the shin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a long vowel and a fatha on the shin; both are dialectal forms, like "al-ra'fah" and "al-ra'afah."

It is in the accusative as a verbal noun, with the extra letters dropped; the original is "al-inshā'ah."

﴿He punishes whom He wills and has mercy on whom He wills﴾, meaning: after the final creation He punishes whom He wills to punish, namely the disbelievers and the disobedient, and has mercy on whom He wills, namely the believers in Him, who confirm His messengers and act upon His commands and prohibitions. ﴿And to Him you will be turned﴾, meaning: you will be returned and brought back, not to any other.

﴿And you cannot escape [Allah] in the earth or in the heaven﴾. al-Farra' said: "Nor those in the heaven can escape Allah in it," and he said: it is like the saying of Hassan:
"Whoever among you satirizes the Messenger of Allah, and whoever praises and supports him, are equal."
meaning: whoever praises and supports him is equal.

Similar to it is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ [al-Saffat: 164], meaning: none but one who has a known station. The meaning is that neither the people of the earth nor the people of the heaven can overpower Him, glory be to Him, in the heaven, should they disobey Him.

Qutrub said: the meaning of the verse is: "nor in the heaven, even if you were in it," as you say: "So-and-so will not escape me here, nor in Basra," meaning: nor in Basra even if he went there.

al-Mubarrad said: the meaning is "nor those in the heaven," with "man" not being a relative pronoun but an indefinite, and "in the heaven" being an adjective of it; the adjective is placed in the position of the noun modified. 'Ali ibn Sulayman rejected this and said: it is not permissible, and he preferred what Qutrub said.

﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah﴾, where "min" is extra for emphasis, meaning: you have no protector who will befriend you, nor a helper who will support you and repel from you the punishment of Allah.

﴿And those who disbelieved in the signs of Allah and His meeting﴾. The "signs" are either the revealed signs, the cosmic signs, or both. "Disbelieved in the meeting of Allah" means: they denied the resurrection and what follows it, and did not act upon what the messengers of Allah, glory be to Him, informed them of. The demonstrative in His saying "those" refers to the disbelievers in the signs and the meeting; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿they have despaired of My mercy﴾, meaning: they are in this world hopeless of Allah's mercy; what was revealed in the books of Allah and what His messengers told them did not benefit them.

It has also been said: the meaning is that they will despair on the Day of Resurrection of Allah's mercy, which is Paradise.

The meaning is that they despaired of mercy. ﴿And those will have a painful punishment﴾. Allah, glory be to Him, repeated the demonstrative for emphasis, and described the punishment as painful to indicate that it is at the extreme of severity.

﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Kill him or burn him."﴾ This is a return to address Abraham after the interjection of what preceded, of address to Muhammad (ﷺ), according to the view of one who says that His saying "Say, travel through the earth" is address to Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the view that it is address to Abraham (peace be upon him), then the discourse in its context before and after is about Abraham, meaning: some of them said to others during their consultation: "Do to Abraham one of the two matters mentioned," and then they agreed upon burning him. ﴿But Allah saved him from the fire.﴾ He made it cool and safe for him. Indeed in that, that is, in Allah's saving Abraham, are clear signs, meaning: manifest proofs and evident marks of the great power of Allah and the wondrous nature of His making: where they kindled that great fire and threw him into it, yet it did not burn him nor affect him at all, but rather it turned into a state contrary to what is its nature of heat and burning. The believers were specifically mentioned because they are the ones who take heed by the signs of Allah, glory be to Him, while others are heedless of that.

Al-Jumhur read "jawaba qawmihi" in the accusative, as the predicate of "kana," with what follows as its subject. Salim al-Aftas, 'Amr ibn Dinar and al-Hasan read it in the nominative, as the subject of "kana," with what follows in an accusative position as the predicate.

﴿And he said, "You have taken idols besides Allah only as a bond of affection between you in the worldly life"﴾, meaning: Abraham said to his people: for mutual affection among you and connection through your unity in worshipping them, and out of fear that affection among you would vanish if you abandon their worship.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read "mawaddata baynikum," with the nominative "mawaddatu" without tanwin and idafah to "baynikum."

al-A'mash and Ibn Thabbit read "mawaddatun" with the nominative and tanwin.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read "mawaddatan" with the accusative and tanwin, and read "baynakum" as an adverbial of place.

Hamzah and Hafs read "mawaddata" with the accusative, in idafah to "baynikum."

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 14–27 (part 2 of 2):

As for the reading with *raf'* (nominative, *raf'* meaning the nominative case), al-Zajjaj (the grammarian) mentioned two aspects for it. The first is that it is in the predicate of *inna* in *innama attakhadhtum*, and he took *ma* to be descriptive (*mawsufa*). The meaning is: "Indeed, that which you have taken besides Allah as idols is the affection among you."

The second aspect is that it is in the nominative by the omission of a subject, i.e., "it is affection," or "that is affection."

The meaning is that affection is what brought you together in worshipping and taking idols.

It has been said that *mawaddatu* may also be in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), with its predicate being *fi al-hayat al-dunya* ("in the life of this world").

As for the one who read *mawaddatan* with *raf'* and with *tanwin* (nunation), its explanation is like the first reading, with *baynikum* in the accusative as an adverb of place (*zarfiyya*).

As for the one who read *mawaddata* with *nasb* (accusative) without *tanwin*, he made it the object of *attakhadhtum*, and he made *innama* a single particle of restriction (*li al-hasr*). The same applies to the one who read it with accusative and *tanwin*.

It is possible that the accusative in these two readings is because affection is the cause, so it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*). In the reading with *raf'*, the second object of *attakhadhtum* is omitted, meaning "idols, gods." And on the assumption that *ma* in His saying *innama attakhadhtum* is a relative pronoun (*mawsula*), the first object is its pronoun, i.e., *attakhadhtumuhu* ("you took it"), and the second object is *awthanan* ("idols").

﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, some of you will disavow others﴾, i.e., some of those who took idols and worshipped them will disavow the others among them. So the leaders will disown the followers, and the followers will disown the leaders. It has also been said that the meaning is: those who worship idols will disown the idols, and the idols will disown those who worship them.

﴿And some of you will curse others﴾, i.e., each group will curse the other, according to the two explanations mentioned. ﴿And your refuge is the Fire﴾, i.e., the disbelievers. It has been said that the idols are included in this, meaning the Fire is your dwelling place to which you return. ﴿And you will have no helpers﴾ who could rescue you from it by their help to you.

﴿So Lot believed him﴾, i.e., Lot believed in Abraham, and confirmed him in all that he brought. It has been said that he did not believe in him until he saw that the fire did not burn him. Lot was the son of Abraham's brother. ﴿And he said, "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord"﴾. Al-Nakha'i and Qatadah said: the one who said "Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord" is Abraham.

Qatadah said: He emigrated from Kuthaa, which is a village in the region of Kufa, to Harran, then to Syria, and with him were his nephew Lot and his wife Sarah. The meaning is: "Indeed I am emigrating from the land of my people to where I may worship my Lord." ﴿Indeed He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, i.e., the Mighty, whose actions proceed according to the requirements of wisdom.

It has been said that the speaker of ﴿Indeed I am emigrating to my Lord﴾ is Lot. But the first is preferable, because the pronoun in His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ refers to Abraham, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book﴾, and likewise in His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world, and indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾. All these pronouns refer to Abraham without any disagreement. The meaning is that Allah bestowed children upon him: He gave him Isaac as a son to him, and Jacob as a son to his son Isaac, and placed in his descendants prophethood and the Book. So Allah did not send a prophet after Abraham except from his lineage. The word *al-Kitab* (the Book) is singular because the definite article *al-* in it is for the genus, which includes all Books, and what is meant are the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, and the Qur'an. The meaning of ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾ is that he was given children in this world, and Allah informed him that prophethood would continue among them, and that is among the things that comfort his eye and increase his joy. It has also been said that his reward in this world is that the people of all religions claim him and say he is one of them.

It has been said that He gave him in this world good deeds and a good end. ﴿And indeed he is in the Hereafter among the righteous﴾, i.e., among those perfected in righteousness, deserving of full reward and abundant gifts from the Lord, glory be to Him.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah sent Noah when he was forty years old, and he remained among his people for a thousand years less fifty years, calling them to Allah. He lived after the Flood sixty years until people multiplied and spread.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ikrimah, who said: Noah's age before he was sent to his people and after he was sent was one thousand seven hundred years.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Awf ibn Abi Shaddad, who said: Indeed Allah sent Noah to his people when he was three hundred and fifty years old, so he remained among them a thousand years less fifty years. Then he lived after that three hundred and fifty years.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya narrated in his book *Dhamm al-Dunya* (Censure of the World) from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Angel of Death came to Noah and said: "O longest-lived of the prophets, how did you find the world and its pleasures?" He said: "Like a man who entered a house with two doors, stood in the middle of the house for a little while, then left through the other door."

Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And We made it a sign for the worlds﴾, that he said: Allah preserved it as a sign, and it is on al-Judi (a mountain).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And you invent a lie﴾, that he said: "You say falsehood."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying "the final creation," that he said: It is life after death, which is the resurrection.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿So Lot believed him﴾, that he said: "Lot confirmed Abraham."

Abu Ya'la and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Anas, who said: "The first of the Muslims to emigrate to Abyssinia with his family was Uthman ibn Affan. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'May Allah accompany them both. Indeed Uthman is the first to emigrate to Allah with his family after Lot.'"

Ibn Mandah and Ibn Asakir narrated from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Uthman emigrated to Abyssinia, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Indeed he is the first to emigrate after Abraham and Lot.'"

Ibn Asakir, al-Tabarani, and al-Hakim in *al-Kuna* narrated from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Between Uthman and Ruqayyah and Lot there was no emigrant."

Ibn Asakir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: The first to emigrate to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was Uthman ibn Affan, just as Lot emigrated to Abraham.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾, that he said: "They were two sons of Abraham." And regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, he said: "Indeed Allah enjoined upon the people of the religions His religion, so there is no people of any religion but that they claim Abraham and are pleased with him."

These same narrators also narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿And We gave him his reward in this world﴾, that he said: "The good remembrance."

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him, saying: "The righteous child and good praise." As for Ibn Abbas's saying "they were two sons of Abraham," perhaps he means his son and his grandson, since a grandson is in the position of a son. Something like this would not be hidden from someone like Ibn Abbas, for he is the scholar (*hibr*) of this nation. This narration from him is from the narration of al-‘Awfi. In the two Sahihs (of al-Bukhari and Muslim) it is narrated: "Indeed the noble, son of a noble, son of a noble, son of a noble is Joseph ibn Jacob ibn Isaac ibn Abraham."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "Lūṭan" (Lot) is in the accusative, either by coordination with "Nūḥan" (Noah), or with "Ibrāhīm" (Abraham), or by the implied verb "udhkur" (mention).

Al-Kisā'ī said: The meaning is "wa-anjaynā Lūṭan" (and We saved Lot), or "wa-arsalnā Lūṭan" (and We sent Lot), when he said to his people, "Idh" (when) being an adverbial element governed by the agent in "Lūṭ": ﴿Indeed, you commit an immorality⁠﴾. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr read "a-innakum" with the interrogative (hamza), while the rest read it without the interrogative.

Al-fāḥishah (immorality) is the act that is extreme in ugliness. The clause ﴿no one among the worlds has preceded you in it⁠﴾ confirms the perfect ugliness of this act, and that they were unique in it: none of the people, across their different kinds, had preceded them in doing it.

Then He, glorified is He, explained this immorality, saying: ﴿Do you indeed approach men⁠﴾, i.e., you commit sodomy with them, ﴿and cut off the way⁠﴾. It was said: they used to commit this immorality with those travelling who passed by them; when they did this, people abandoned passing by them, so they cut off the way for this reason.

al-Farrā' said: They would intercept people on the roads with their wicked deed. It was also said: they would cut the road upon passersby by killing them and plundering them.

The apparent meaning is that they were doing what would cause the road to be cut, without restriction to a specific cause. It was also said that the meaning of cutting the road is cutting off offspring by turning away from women to men. ﴿And commit the evil⁠﴾ in your assemblies. Al-nādī, al-nadī and al-mundā are the gathering of a people and their place of conversation.

al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related regarding His saying: ﴿So the earthquake seized them⁠﴾ that he said: "The cry." And regarding His saying: "and they were insightful" he said: "in error."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿So of them is one upon whom We sent a storm of stones﴾, that he said: the people of Lut. ﴿And of them is one who was seized by the blast﴾, he said: Thamud. ﴿And of them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾, he said: Qarun. ﴿And of them is one whom We drowned﴾, he said: the people of Nuh.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "Lūṭan" (Lot) is in the accusative, either by coordination with "Nūḥan" (Noah), or with "Ibrāhīm" (Abraham), or by the implied verb "udhkur" (mention).

Al-Kisā'ī said: The meaning is "wa-anjaynā Lūṭan" (and We saved Lot), or "wa-arsalnā Lūṭan" (and We sent Lot), when he said to his people, "Idh" (when) being an adverbial element governed by the agent in "Lūṭ": ﴿Indeed, you commit an immorality⁠﴾. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr read "a-innakum" with the interrogative (hamza), while the rest read it without the interrogative.

Al-fāḥishah (immorality) is the act that is extreme in ugliness. The clause ﴿no one among the worlds has preceded you in it⁠﴾ confirms the perfect ugliness of this act, and that they were unique in it: none of the people, across their different kinds, had preceded them in doing it.

Then He, glorified is He, explained this immorality, saying: ﴿Do you indeed approach men⁠﴾, i.e., you commit sodomy with them, ﴿and cut off the way⁠﴾. It was said: they used to commit this immorality with those travelling who passed by them; when they did this, people abandoned passing by them, so they cut off the way for this reason.

al-Farrā' said: They would intercept people on the roads with their wicked deed. It was also said: they would cut the road upon passersby by killing them and plundering them.

The apparent meaning is that they were doing what would cause the road to be cut, without restriction to a specific cause. It was also said that the meaning of cutting the road is cutting off offspring by turning away from women to men. ﴿And commit the evil⁠﴾ in your assemblies. Al-nādī, al-nadī and al-mundā are the gathering of a people and their place of conversation.

They differed about the evil (munkar) they used to commit in their assemblies. It was said: they would pelt people with pebbles and mock strangers. It was said: they would break wind in their gatherings. It was said: they would commit sodomy with men in their gatherings while others watched. It was said: they would play with pigeons. It was said: they would dye their fingers with henna. It was said: they would set cocks to fight and rams to butt each other. It was said: they would play backgammon and chess and wear dyed garments. There is no barrier to their having committed all of these abominations.

al-Zajjāj said: In this there is an indication that people should not associate with one another in wrongdoing, nor gather for mockery and forbidden things.

When Lot denounced to them what they were doing, they replied with what God related of them in His saying: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of God, if you are of the truthful⁠﴾. That is: they answered with nothing but this statement, returning to denial, obstinacy and stubbornness. The discussion of this verse has already passed, and it was discussed earlier in Surat al-Naml: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your town"⁠﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and in Surat al-A‘rāf: ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town"⁠﴾ [al-A‘rāf: 82]. These three places are reconciled by saying that Lot remained steadfast in guidance and repeatedly forbade them and warned them. So they first said to him: "Bring us the punishment of God," as in this verse. When he persisted in this and did not remain silent about them, they said: "Expel them," as in al-A‘rāf and al-Naml. It was also said: they first said, "Expel them from your town," then they said secondly, "Bring us the punishment of God."

Then, when Lot despaired of them, he sought victory over them from God, glorified is He, so he ﴿said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people⁠﴾, by sending down Your punishment upon them. Their corruption is by what has preceded of approaching men and committing the evil in their assemblies. God, glorified is He, responded and sent His angels for their punishment, and commanded them to give Abraham good tidings before their punishment.

Therefore He said: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings⁠﴾, that is, with the good tiding of a son, Isaac, and of a son's son, Jacob. ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town⁠﴾, that is, they said this statement to Abraham. The town is the town of Sodom in which the people of Lot dwelt. The clause ﴿Indeed, its people have been wrongdoers⁠﴾ is a reason for the destruction, that is, Our destroying them is for this cause.

﴿He said, "Indeed, Lot is there⁠﴾, that is, Abraham said to them: "Indeed, in this town which you are going to destroy is Lot. How will you destroy it?" ﴿They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it⁠﴾ of the righteous and the wicked, and we know better than others the place of Lot, ﴿we will surely save him and his family⁠﴾ from the punishment.

al-A‘mash, Ḥamzah, Ya‘qūb and al-Kisā'ī read "la-nunjiyannahu" with light (tashdīd-less) pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis. ﴿Except his wife; she was of those who remained behind⁠﴾, that is, those who remained in the punishment. This is a word shared between the past and the remaining, and its exact analysis has already passed. It was also said the meaning is: among those who remained in the town on which the punishment would descend, so she would be punished among them and would not be saved along with those who were saved.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them⁠﴾, that is: when the messengers came to Lot after parting from Abraham, he was distressed for them, that is, what displeased him came upon him and he feared for them, because he thought them to be human, so he feared for them from his people, since they were in the finest form of human appearance. The "an" in "an jā'at" is superfluous, for emphasis. ﴿And he was straitened by them⁠﴾, that is, he was unable to manage them, grieved and his chest constricted. Constriction of the arm is a metaphor for inability, just as one says, in metaphor for poverty, "his hand was constricted." The explanation of this has been given fully in Surat Hūd.

When the angels saw what had befallen him of grief and distress, ﴿they said, "Fear not, nor grieve⁠﴾, that is: do not fear for us from your people, nor grieve, for they cannot prevail over us. ﴿Indeed, we will save you and your family⁠﴾ from the punishment which God has commanded us to send down upon them, ﴿except your wife; she was of those who remained behind⁠﴾. They informed Lot of what they had come with, the destruction of his people and the saving of him and his family except his wife, just as they informed Abraham of this. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Shu‘bah, Ya‘qūb and al-A‘mash read "munajjūka" with light pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis.

al-Mubarrad said: The kāf in "munajjūka" is in the genitive, and it was not permissible to coordinate a noun with a pronominal suffix in the genitive, so the second was understood according to the meaning, and the sense becomes: "and We will save your family."

﴿Indeed, We are sending down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky⁠﴾. This clause is resumptive, explaining their destruction, which is understood from specifying the salvation of him and his family. Rijz (punishment) is torment; that is, a punishment from the sky, which is the pelting with stones. It was said: their burning with a fire descending from the sky. It was said: it is the sinking and the stoning, as in other places. The meaning of the sinking being "from the sky" is that the command for it descended from the sky.

Ibn ʿĀmir read "munazzilūna" with emphasis, and Ibn ʿAbbās read it so as well. The rest read it with light pronunciation. The "bi" in "bi-mā kānū yafsuqūn" is causal: that is, because of their wickedness.

﴿And We have left from it a clear sign⁠﴾, that is, We left from the town a clear sign and proof, namely the traces of the stones with which they were pelted and the ruin of their dwellings.

Mujāhid said: it is the black water remaining on the face of their land. There is no barrier to applying the verse to all that has been mentioned. The statement is specified to "people who understand," because it is they who grasp that these traces are a lesson which whoever sees them may take heed of.

﴿And to Madyan (We sent) their brother Shu‘ayb⁠﴾, that is, We sent him to them. His mention, his lineage and his people have already been discussed in Surat al-A‘rāf and Surat Hūd. ﴿He said, "O my people, worship God⁠﴾, that is: single Him out in worship and devote worship to Him, ﴿and hope for the Last Day⁠﴾, that is: expect it, and do today the deeds that will ward off His punishment from you.

Yūnus al-Naḥwī said: its meaning is: fear the Hereafter, in which there is recompense for deeds. ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption⁠﴾. al-ʿAth̲w̲ (abuse) is the worst kind of corruption. Its explanation has already passed.

﴿So the earthquake seized them⁠﴾, that is, the quake, as already discussed in Surat Hūd. ﴿And the blast seized those who did wrong⁠﴾ [Hūd: 67], that is, the cry of Gabriel, which was the cause of the quake. ﴿So they became, in their home, prostrate⁠﴾, that is: they became in their land or their dwellings, prostrate on their knees, dead.

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd⁠﴾. al-Kisā'ī said: Some said it refers back to the beginning of the surah, that is: "And We certainly tested those before them, and We tested ʿĀd and Thamūd." He said: The more beloved to me is that it be read as "So the earthquake seized them," that is: "and it seized ʿĀd and Thamūd."

al-Zajjāj said: The estimate is: "and We destroyed ʿĀd and Thamūd." It was also said: the meaning is: "and mention ʿĀd and Thamūd, when We sent to them Hūd and Ṣāliḥ." ﴿And it has become clear to you from their dwellings⁠﴾, that is: and there has appeared to you, O company of disbelievers, from their dwellings in al-Ḥijr and al-Aḥqāf, clear signs by which you may take heed and reflect. The subject of "tabayyana" is thus omitted. ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them⁠﴾, which they were doing of disbelief and disobedience to God. Thus he turned them by this adornment away from the path, that is, the clear way leading to the truth, while they were ⁠﴾mustabṣirīn⁠﴾, that is, people of insight by which they could attain knowledge of the truth through reasoning.

al-Farrā' said: They were intelligent people of insight, but their insight did not benefit them. It was also said: the meaning is: they were insightful in their disbelief and error, admiring it, thinking themselves upon guidance and seeing their affair as true. So He described them as insightful in this sense, with reference to what they had in themselves.

﴿And Qārūn and Pharaoh and Hāmān⁠﴾. al-Kisā'ī said: If you wish, it is governed by "ʿĀd", and there is in it what there is; and if you wish, it is governed by "faṣaddahum ʿan al-sabīl", that is: "and [Satan] turned away Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān."

It was also said: the estimate is: "and We destroyed these after the messengers had come to them, and they were arrogant in the earth, rejecting the worship of God. And they were not ones who could escape (sābiqīn)," that is, they could not outrun Him. It is said: "sabaqa ṭālibahu" when he escaped the seeker. It was also said: "and they were not ones who preceded in disbelief," for many generations had preceded them in it.

﴿So each We seized for his sin⁠﴾, that is: We punished each for his disbelief and denial.

al-Kisā'ī said: "fa-kullan akhadhnā" means "fa-akhadhnā kullan bi-dhanbihi" (so We seized each for his sin). ﴿Then among them is one upon whom We sent a hāṣib⁠﴾, that is, a wind bringing pebbles, the small stones, which pelted them with them, and they were the people of Lot. ﴿And among them is one whom the blast seized⁠﴾, and they were Thamūd and the people of Madyan. ﴿And among them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow⁠﴾, and he was Qārūn and his companions. ﴿And among them is one whom We drowned⁠﴾, and they were the people of Noah and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿And God would not wrong them⁠﴾ by what He did to them, because He had sent His messengers to them and sent down His scriptures upon them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves⁠﴾ by persisting in disbelief, denying the messengers and doing the disobedience of God.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾, that he said: "your gathering."

He said: They used to sit on the road, pelting the sons of the road and mocking them."

al-Tirmidhī said after relating it and grading it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Ḥātim ibn Abī Ṣaghīrah from Simāk."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jābir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade pelting," and this is the saying of God, glorified is He: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾.

How will you destroy it?" ﴿They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it⁠﴾ of the righteous and the wicked, and we know better than others the place of Lot, ﴿we will surely save him and his family⁠﴾ from the punishment.

This is a word shared between the past and the remaining, and its exact analysis has already passed. It was also said the meaning is: among those who remained in the town on which the punishment would descend, so she would be punished among them and would not be saved along with those who were saved.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "Lūṭan" (Lot) is in the accusative, either by coordination with "Nūḥan" (Noah), or with "Ibrāhīm" (Abraham), or by the implied verb "udhkur" (mention).

Al-Kisā'ī said: The meaning is "wa-anjaynā Lūṭan" (and We saved Lot), or "wa-arsalnā Lūṭan" (and We sent Lot), when he said to his people, "Idh" (when) being an adverbial element governed by the agent in "Lūṭ": ﴿Indeed, you commit an immorality⁠﴾. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr read "a-innakum" with the interrogative (hamza), while the rest read it without the interrogative.

Al-fāḥishah (immorality) is the act that is extreme in ugliness. The clause ﴿no one among the worlds has preceded you in it⁠﴾ confirms the perfect ugliness of this act, and that they were unique in it: none of the people, across their different kinds, had preceded them in doing it.

Then He, glorified is He, explained this immorality, saying: ﴿Do you indeed approach men⁠﴾, i.e., you commit sodomy with them, ﴿and cut off the way⁠﴾. It was said: they used to commit this immorality with those travelling who passed by them; when they did this, people abandoned passing by them, so they cut off the way for this reason.

al-Farrā' said: They would intercept people on the roads with their wicked deed. It was also said: they would cut the road upon passersby by killing them and plundering them.

The apparent meaning is that they were doing what would cause the road to be cut, without restriction to a specific cause. It was also said that the meaning of cutting the road is cutting off offspring by turning away from women to men. ﴿And commit the evil⁠﴾ in your assemblies. Al-nādī, al-nadī and al-mundā are the gathering of a people and their place of conversation.

They differed about the evil (munkar) they used to commit in their assemblies. It was said: they would pelt people with pebbles and mock strangers. It was said: they would break wind in their gatherings. It was said: they would commit sodomy with men in their gatherings while others watched. It was said: they would play with pigeons. It was said: they would dye their fingers with henna. It was said: they would set cocks to fight and rams to butt each other. It was said: they would play backgammon and chess and wear dyed garments. There is no barrier to their having committed all of these abominations.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verses 28–40 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: "Lūṭan" (Lot) is in the accusative, either by coordination with "Nūḥan" (Noah), or with "Ibrāhīm" (Abraham), or by the implied verb "udhkur" (mention).

Al-Kisā'ī said: The meaning is "wa-anjaynā Lūṭan" (and We saved Lot), or "wa-arsalnā Lūṭan" (and We sent Lot), when he said to his people, "Idh" (when) being an adverbial element governed by the agent in "Lūṭ": ﴿Indeed, you commit an immorality⁠﴾. Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and Abū Bakr read "a-innakum" with the interrogative (hamza), while the rest read it without the interrogative.

Al-fāḥishah (immorality) is the act that is extreme in ugliness. The clause ﴿no one among the worlds has preceded you in it⁠﴾ confirms the perfect ugliness of this act, and that they were unique in it: none of the people, across their different kinds, had preceded them in doing it.

Then He, glorified is He, explained this immorality, saying: ﴿Do you indeed approach men⁠﴾, i.e., you commit sodomy with them, ﴿and cut off the way⁠﴾. It was said: they used to commit this immorality with those travelling who passed by them; when they did this, people abandoned passing by them, so they cut off the way for this reason.

al-Farrā' said: They would intercept people on the roads with their wicked deed. It was also said: they would cut the road upon passersby by killing them and plundering them.

The apparent meaning is that they were doing what would cause the road to be cut, without restriction to a specific cause. It was also said that the meaning of cutting the road is cutting off offspring by turning away from women to men. ﴿And commit the evil⁠﴾ in your assemblies. Al-nādī, al-nadī and al-mundā are the gathering of a people and their place of conversation.

They differed about the evil (munkar) they used to commit in their assemblies. It was said: they would pelt people with pebbles and mock strangers. It was said: they would break wind in their gatherings. It was said: they would commit sodomy with men in their gatherings while others watched. It was said: they would play with pigeons. It was said: they would dye their fingers with henna. It was said: they would set cocks to fight and rams to butt each other. It was said: they would play backgammon and chess and wear dyed garments. There is no barrier to their having committed all of these abominations.

al-Zajjāj said: In this there is an indication that people should not associate with one another in wrongdoing, nor gather for mockery and forbidden things.

When Lot denounced to them what they were doing, they replied with what God related of them in His saying: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Bring us the punishment of God, if you are of the truthful⁠﴾. That is: they answered with nothing but this statement, returning to denial, obstinacy and stubbornness. The discussion of this verse has already passed, and it was discussed earlier in Surat al-Naml: ﴿So the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel the family of Lot from your town"⁠﴾ [al-Naml: 56], and in Surat al-A‘rāf: ﴿And the answer of his people was only that they said, "Expel them from your town"⁠﴾ [al-A‘rāf: 82]. These three places are reconciled by saying that Lot remained steadfast in guidance and repeatedly forbade them and warned them. So they first said to him: "Bring us the punishment of God," as in this verse. When he persisted in this and did not remain silent about them, they said: "Expel them," as in al-A‘rāf and al-Naml. It was also said: they first said, "Expel them from your town," then they said secondly, "Bring us the punishment of God."

Then, when Lot despaired of them, he sought victory over them from God, glorified is He, so he ﴿said, "My Lord, help me against the corrupt people⁠﴾, by sending down Your punishment upon them. Their corruption is by what has preceded of approaching men and committing the evil in their assemblies. God, glorified is He, responded and sent His angels for their punishment, and commanded them to give Abraham good tidings before their punishment.

Therefore He said: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Abraham with good tidings⁠﴾, that is, with the good tiding of a son, Isaac, and of a son's son, Jacob. ﴿They said, "Indeed, we are going to destroy the people of this town⁠﴾, that is, they said this statement to Abraham. The town is the town of Sodom in which the people of Lot dwelt. The clause ﴿Indeed, its people have been wrongdoers⁠﴾ is a reason for the destruction, that is, Our destroying them is for this cause.

﴿He said, "Indeed, Lot is there⁠﴾, that is, Abraham said to them: "Indeed, in this town which you are going to destroy is Lot. How will you destroy it?" ﴿They said, "We are most knowing of who is in it⁠﴾ of the righteous and the wicked, and we know better than others the place of Lot, ﴿we will surely save him and his family⁠﴾ from the punishment.

al-A‘mash, Ḥamzah, Ya‘qūb and al-Kisā'ī read "la-nunjiyannahu" with light (tashdīd-less) pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis. ﴿Except his wife; she was of those who remained behind⁠﴾, that is, those who remained in the punishment. This is a word shared between the past and the remaining, and its exact analysis has already passed. It was also said the meaning is: among those who remained in the town on which the punishment would descend, so she would be punished among them and would not be saved along with those who were saved.

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed for them⁠﴾, that is: when the messengers came to Lot after parting from Abraham, he was distressed for them, that is, what displeased him came upon him and he feared for them, because he thought them to be human, so he feared for them from his people, since they were in the finest form of human appearance. The "an" in "an jā'at" is superfluous, for emphasis. ﴿And he was straitened by them⁠﴾, that is, he was unable to manage them, grieved and his chest constricted. Constriction of the arm is a metaphor for inability, just as one says, in metaphor for poverty, "his hand was constricted." The explanation of this has been given fully in Surat Hūd.

When the angels saw what had befallen him of grief and distress, ﴿they said, "Fear not, nor grieve⁠﴾, that is: do not fear for us from your people, nor grieve, for they cannot prevail over us. ﴿Indeed, we will save you and your family⁠﴾ from the punishment which God has commanded us to send down upon them, ﴿except your wife; she was of those who remained behind⁠﴾. They informed Lot of what they had come with, the destruction of his people and the saving of him and his family except his wife, just as they informed Abraham of this. Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Shu‘bah, Ya‘qūb and al-A‘mash read "munajjūka" with light pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis.

al-Mubarrad said: The kāf in "munajjūka" is in the genitive, and it was not permissible to coordinate a noun with a pronominal suffix in the genitive, so the second was understood according to the meaning, and the sense becomes: "and We will save your family."

﴿Indeed, We are sending down upon the people of this town a punishment from the sky⁠﴾. This clause is resumptive, explaining their destruction, which is understood from specifying the salvation of him and his family. Rijz (punishment) is torment; that is, a punishment from the sky, which is the pelting with stones. It was said: their burning with a fire descending from the sky. It was said: it is the sinking and the stoning, as in other places. The meaning of the sinking being "from the sky" is that the command for it descended from the sky.

Ibn ʿĀmir read "munazzilūna" with emphasis, and Ibn ʿAbbās read it so as well. The rest read it with light pronunciation. The "bi" in "bi-mā kānū yafsuqūn" is causal: that is, because of their wickedness.

﴿And We have left from it a clear sign⁠﴾, that is, We left from the town a clear sign and proof, namely the traces of the stones with which they were pelted and the ruin of their dwellings.

Mujāhid said: it is the black water remaining on the face of their land. There is no barrier to applying the verse to all that has been mentioned. The statement is specified to "people who understand," because it is they who grasp that these traces are a lesson which whoever sees them may take heed of.

﴿And to Madyan (We sent) their brother Shu‘ayb⁠﴾, that is, We sent him to them. His mention, his lineage and his people have already been discussed in Surat al-A‘rāf and Surat Hūd. ﴿He said, "O my people, worship God⁠﴾, that is: single Him out in worship and devote worship to Him, ﴿and hope for the Last Day⁠﴾, that is: expect it, and do today the deeds that will ward off His punishment from you.

Yūnus al-Naḥwī said: its meaning is: fear the Hereafter, in which there is recompense for deeds. ﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, spreading corruption⁠﴾. al-ʿAth̲w̲ (abuse) is the worst kind of corruption. Its explanation has already passed.

﴿So the earthquake seized them⁠﴾, that is, the quake, as already discussed in Surat Hūd. ﴿And the blast seized those who did wrong⁠﴾ [Hūd: 67], that is, the cry of Gabriel, which was the cause of the quake. ﴿So they became, in their home, prostrate⁠﴾, that is: they became in their land or their dwellings, prostrate on their knees, dead.

﴿And ʿĀd and Thamūd⁠﴾. al-Kisā'ī said: Some said it refers back to the beginning of the surah, that is: "And We certainly tested those before them, and We tested ʿĀd and Thamūd." He said: The more beloved to me is that it be read as "So the earthquake seized them," that is: "and it seized ʿĀd and Thamūd."

al-Zajjāj said: The estimate is: "and We destroyed ʿĀd and Thamūd." It was also said: the meaning is: "and mention ʿĀd and Thamūd, when We sent to them Hūd and Ṣāliḥ." ﴿And it has become clear to you from their dwellings⁠﴾, that is: and there has appeared to you, O company of disbelievers, from their dwellings in al-Ḥijr and al-Aḥqāf, clear signs by which you may take heed and reflect. The subject of "tabayyana" is thus omitted. ﴿And Satan made their deeds appealing to them⁠﴾, which they were doing of disbelief and disobedience to God. Thus he turned them by this adornment away from the path, that is, the clear way leading to the truth, while they were ⁠﴾mustabṣirīn⁠﴾, that is, people of insight by which they could attain knowledge of the truth through reasoning.

al-Farrā' said: They were intelligent people of insight, but their insight did not benefit them. It was also said: the meaning is: they were insightful in their disbelief and error, admiring it, thinking themselves upon guidance and seeing their affair as true. So He described them as insightful in this sense, with reference to what they had in themselves.

﴿And Qārūn and Pharaoh and Hāmān⁠﴾. al-Kisā'ī said: If you wish, it is governed by "ʿĀd", and there is in it what there is; and if you wish, it is governed by "faṣaddahum ʿan al-sabīl", that is: "and [Satan] turned away Qārūn, Pharaoh and Hāmān."

It was also said: the estimate is: "and We destroyed these after the messengers had come to them, and they were arrogant in the earth, rejecting the worship of God. And they were not ones who could escape (sābiqīn)," that is, they could not outrun Him. It is said: "sabaqa ṭālibahu" when he escaped the seeker. It was also said: "and they were not ones who preceded in disbelief," for many generations had preceded them in it.

﴿So each We seized for his sin⁠﴾, that is: We punished each for his disbelief and denial.

al-Kisā'ī said: "fa-kullan akhadhnā" means "fa-akhadhnā kullan bi-dhanbihi" (so We seized each for his sin). ﴿Then among them is one upon whom We sent a hāṣib⁠﴾, that is, a wind bringing pebbles, the small stones, which pelted them with them, and they were the people of Lot. ﴿And among them is one whom the blast seized⁠﴾, and they were Thamūd and the people of Madyan. ﴿And among them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow⁠﴾, and he was Qārūn and his companions. ﴿And among them is one whom We drowned⁠﴾, and they were the people of Noah and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿And God would not wrong them⁠﴾ by what He did to them, because He had sent His messengers to them and sent down His scriptures upon them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves⁠﴾ by persisting in disbelief, denying the messengers and doing the disobedience of God.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾, that he said: "your gathering."

al-Firyābī, Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Kitāb al-Ṣamt, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab and Ibn ʿAsākir related from Umm Hāni' bint Abī Ṭālib, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the saying of God, glorified is He: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾. He said: They used to sit on the road, pelting the sons of the road and mocking them."

al-Tirmidhī said after relating it and grading it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Ḥātim ibn Abī Ṣaghīrah from Simāk."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jābir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade pelting," and this is the saying of God, glorified is He: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿUmar regarding the verse that he said: "It is pelting." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿĀ'ishah regarding the verse that she said: "It is flatulence."

al-Kisā'ī said: "fa-kullan akhadhnā" means "fa-akhadhnā kullan bi-dhanbihi" (so We seized each for his sin). ﴿Then among them is one upon whom We sent a hāṣib⁠﴾, that is, a wind bringing pebbles, the small stones, which pelted them with them, and they were the people of Lot. ﴿And among them is one whom the blast seized⁠﴾, and they were Thamūd and the people of Madyan. ﴿And among them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow⁠﴾, and he was Qārūn and his companions. ﴿And among them is one whom We drowned⁠﴾, and they were the people of Noah and the people of Pharaoh. ﴿And God would not wrong them⁠﴾ by what He did to them, because He had sent His messengers to them and sent down His scriptures upon them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves⁠﴾ by persisting in disbelief, denying the messengers and doing the disobedience of God.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from Ibn ʿAbbās, regarding His saying: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾, that he said: "your gathering."

al-Firyābī, Aḥmad, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan, Ibn Abī al-Dunyā in Kitāb al-Ṣamt, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, al-Ḥākim, who authenticated it, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab and Ibn ʿAsākir related from Umm Hāni' bint Abī Ṭālib, who said: "I asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about the saying of God, glorified is He: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾. He said: They used to sit on the road, pelting the sons of the road and mocking them."

al-Tirmidhī said after relating it and grading it: "We do not know it except from the hadith of Ḥātim ibn Abī Ṣaghīrah from Simāk."

Ibn Mardawayh related from Jābir that "the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade pelting," and this is the saying of God, glorified is He: ﴿And commit the evil in your assemblies⁠﴾.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿUmar regarding the verse that he said: "It is pelting." ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd related the like of it from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Bukhārī in his Tārīkh, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh related from ʿĀ'ishah regarding the verse that she said: "It is flatulence."

al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related regarding His saying: ﴿So the earthquake seized them⁠﴾ that he said: "The cry." And regarding His saying: "and they were insightful" he said: "in error."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿So of them is one upon whom We sent a storm of stones﴾, that he said: the people of Lut. ﴿And of them is one who was seized by the blast﴾, he said: Thamud. ﴿And of them is one whom We caused the earth to swallow﴾, he said: Qarun. ﴿And of them is one whom We drowned﴾, he said: the people of Nuh.

(p-1121) **His saying:** ﴿The likeness of those who take other than Allah as protectors﴾ means those who make them allies and rely on them for their needs, apart from Allah, whether they are inanimate objects or animals, living or dead. ﴿Is like the spider that takes a house﴾. Indeed, its house does not benefit it at all, neither against heat, nor cold, nor rain. Likewise, what they have taken as a protector besides Allah does not benefit them in any way of benefit and does not avail them anything.

Al-Farra' said: This is a parable that Allah has coined for one who takes other gods besides Him, which do not benefit or harm him, just as the spider's house does not shield it from heat or cold.

He said: It is not good to stop at "al-'Ankabut" (the spider), because when the comparison is made to its house, which does not shield it from anything, the gods that neither benefit nor harm are compared to it. Al-Akhfash permitted pausing at "al-'Ankabut," but Ibn al-Anbari considered this an error, saying: "Because *ittakhadhat* (took) is a *silah* (relative clause) of *al-'Ankabut*, as if he had said: 'Like the spider that took a house.' So it is not good to stop at the *silah* without the *mawsul* (the relative pronoun/noun it modifies)." *Al-'Ankabut* applies to the singular and plural, masculine and feminine. Its plurals are *'anakib* and *'ankabutat*. It is a small insect that weaves a fine web. It is also said: *la-ha 'akanbat*, and from this is the poet's verse:

> As if there falls from its saliva
> A house of spider-webs upon its bridle.

﴿And indeed the weakest of houses is the house of the spider﴾: there is no house weaker than it among what insects take as a house, and nothing comes close to it in frailty and fragility, if they only knew that taking protectors besides Allah is like the spider taking a house. Or if they knew anything of knowledge, they would have known this.

﴿Indeed, Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him of anything﴾: *ma* may be interrogative, negative, or relative, and *min* may be partitive or emphatic (*zā'idah li-l-ta'kīd*).

It was also said that this sentence is governed by an implied "say" (*idmar al-qawl*), meaning: "Say to the disbelievers: Indeed Allah knows whatever they call upon besides Him."

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi affirmed that it is interrogative. On the basis of a negative, it is as if it were said: "Indeed Allah knows that you do not call upon anything besides Him," meaning: what you call upon is not a thing. On the basis of a relative, it means: "Indeed Allah knows those whom you call upon besides Him." It is also permissible for *ma* to be a verbal noun (*maṣdariyyah*), and *min shay'* would then be an expression for the verbal noun.

ʿĀṣim, Abu ʿAmr, and Yaʿqub read *yad'ūna* with the third person (*bi-l-taḥtiyyah*). Abu ʿUbayd preferred this reading because the peoples were mentioned before this verse. The rest read it with the second person (*bi-l-fawqiyyah*), as addressed speech. ﴿And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾: the Victorious, the Wise, who brings His actions to the utmost degree of perfection and precision.

﴿And these parables We coin for the people﴾: that is, this parable and others like it in the Qur'an, which We coin for people as a warning to them and to bring closer to their understanding what is far from it. ﴿And none understand them except the knowledgeable﴾, that is, none understand and comprehend the matter for which We coined them except those who know Allah, the firmly rooted in knowledge, who reflect and contemplate what is recited to them and what they witness.

﴿Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾: that is, with justice and equity, taking into account in their creation the welfare of His servants.

It was also said: The meaning of "truth" is His speech and His power. The position of *bi-l-ḥaqq* is accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). ﴿Indeed in that is a sign for the believers﴾: that is, indeed there is a great proof and a manifest indication of His power and His singularity in divinity. He specified the believers because they are the ones who benefit from it.

﴿Recite what has been revealed to you of the Book﴾: that is, the Qur'an. In it is the command to recite the Qur'an, to be steadfast in reading it, reflecting on its verses and contemplating its meanings. ﴿And establish prayer. Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾: that is, persist in establishing it and continue in performing it as you have been commanded. The clause ﴿indeed prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ is a reason for what precedes it. *Al-fahshā'* is what is ugly of deeds, and *al-munkar* is what is not recognized in the Sharia. That is, it prevents one from the disobedience of Allah and keeps one away from it. The meaning of its prohibiting this is that performing it is a cause for refraining. What is intended here is the obligatory prayers. ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾: that is, greater than everything, meaning more excellent than all acts of worship without remembrance.

Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: In my view the meaning is: "And the remembrance of Allah is greater" absolutely, that is, it is what prohibits immorality and wrongdoing. So the part of it that occurs during prayer does this, and it also does what does not occur in prayer, because refraining only comes from one who remembers Allah and is mindful of Him.

It was also said: The remembrance of Allah is greater than prayer in forbidding immorality and wrongdoing, together with its constancy. Al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah said: What is meant by "remembrance" in the verse is glorification (*tasbīḥ*) and declaration of His oneness (*tahlīl*). One says: He is greater, and more worthy of forbidding immorality and wrongdoing.

It was also said: What is meant by "remembrance" here is prayer, that is, prayer is greater than the rest of the acts of obedience. He expressed it as "remembrance," as in His saying: ﴿So hasten to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 9], to indicate that the remembrance it contains is the principal basis for its superiority over the rest of the acts of obedience.

It was also said: The meaning is: And the remembrance of Allah toward you, with reward and praise from Him upon you, is greater than your remembrance of Him in your worship and your prayers. Ibn Jarir chose this view, and it is supported by the hadith: "Whoever remembers Me in himself, I remember him in Myself, and whoever remembers Me in an assembly, I remember him in an assembly better than them." ﴿And Allah knows what you do﴾: nothing of that is hidden from Him, so He will recompense you with good for good and with evil for evil.

﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the best manner﴾: that is, except with the way that is best. This is by way of calling them to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and drawing their attention to His proofs and evidences, hoping they will respond by embracing Islam, not by way of harshness and roughness. ﴿Except those of them who have wronged﴾: that is, by going to excess in argument and not behaving courteously toward the Muslims. There is then no harm in being harsh with them and rough in arguing with them. Thus most exegetes explained the verse, that the People of the Book meant the Jews and the Christians.

It was also said: The meaning of the verse is: Do not argue with those among the People of the Book who believed in Muhammad, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and all others among them who believed, except in the best manner, meaning by agreeing with what they tell you of the reports of the People of the Book. According to this view, those "who have wronged" are those who remained upon their disbelief.

It was also said: This verse is abrogated (*mansūkhah*) by the verses of fighting (*āyāt al-qitāl*). Qatadah and Muqatil said so. Al-Nahhas said: Whoever says it is abrogated argues that the verse is Meccan, and at that time there was no obligatory fighting, nor demand for the poll-tax (*jizyah*), nor anything else of that kind.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: What is meant by "those of them who have wronged" are those who took up war against the Muslims, so arguing with them is by the sword until they embrace Islam or pay the poll-tax. ﴿And say: We believe in what has been revealed to us﴾ of the Qur'an, ﴿and what has been revealed to you (p-1122) of the Torah and the Gospel﴾, that is: we believe that both are sent down from Allah, and that they are a law that remains valid until the establishment of the Islamic law and the mission of Muhammad. This does not include what they have distorted and altered. ﴿Our God and your God is one﴾, having no partner, no equal, and no rival. ﴿And we are Muslims to Him﴾: that is, we, the community of Muhammad, obey Him exclusively. We did not say that ʿUzayr is the son of Allah, nor that the Messiah is the son of Allah, nor did we take our rabbis and monks as lords besides Allah. It is also possible that what is meant is: "and we are all submitting to Him." That this interpretation considers the submission of the Muslims more complete than the submission of the People of the Book, and their obedience more emphatic than theirs, does not weaken this meaning.

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who take other than Allah as protectors﴾, the verse, that he said: That is a parable Allah coined for one who worships other than Him: his likeness is like the likeness of the spider's house.

Abu Dawud reported in his *Marasil* from Yazid ibn Marthad, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The spider is a devil whom Allah transformed. Whoever finds it, let him kill it."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Mazid ibn Maysarah, who said: The spider is a devil.

Al-Khatib reported from ʿAli, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I and Abu Bakr entered the cave, and the spiders gathered and wove at the entrance, so do not kill them."

Al-Qurtubi related in his *Tafsir* from ʿAli also, that he said: Clean your houses of spider-webs, for leaving it in the house brings poverty.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from ʿAta' al-Khurasani, who said: The spider wove twice: once over Dawud, and a second time over the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾, that he said: In prayer there is a restraint and a deterrent from sins.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh reported from ʿImran ibn Husayn, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the saying of Allah: ﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾, and he said: "Whoever his prayer does not forbid immorality and wrongdoing, there is no prayer for him."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever his prayer does not forbid immorality and wrongdoing, he increases in nothing through it from Allah except distance."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever his prayer does not forbid immorality and wrongdoing, there is no prayer for him." In another wording: "He does not increase through it from Allah except distance."

Al-Khatib reported from Ibn ʿUmar, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Masʿud, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar. Al-Suyuti said: Its chain is weak.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ahmad in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Tabarani in *al-Shuʿab* reported something similar from him as a statement of his own (*mawquf*).

Ibn Kathir said in his *Tafsir*: The most authentic of all of this are the statements (*mawqufat*) from Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Aʿmash, and others.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding His saying: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾, that he said: The remembrance of Allah of His servants, when they remember Him, is greater than their remembrance of Him.

Al-Firyabi, Sa'd ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Shuʿab* reported from ʿAbd Allah ibn Rabiʿah, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas asked me about the saying of Allah: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾. I said: The remembrance of Allah is by glorification, declaration of His oneness, and magnification. He said: The remembrance of Allah of you is greater than your remembrance of Him. Then he said: "Remember Me, and I will remember you."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd*, and Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn Masʿud regarding ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾, that he said: The remembrance of Allah of the servant is greater than the remembrance of the servant of Allah.

Ibn al-Sunni, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Daylami reported something similar from Ibn ʿUmar.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding the verse, that he said: It has two aspects: the remembrance of Allah is greater than anything else. In another wording: the remembrance of Allah at what He has forbidden, and the remembrance of Allah of you is greater than your remembrance of Him.

Ahmad in *al-Zuhd* and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Muʿadh ibn Jabal, who said: No human has performed any deed that is more saving for him from the punishment of Allah than the remembrance of Allah. They said: Not even jihad in the path of Allah? He said: Not even if he strikes with his sword until it breaks, because Allah says in His Mighty Book: ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 29, verse 41–46 (part 2 of 2):

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim in al-Kuna, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from 'Anbasah, who said: I said to Ibn 'Abbas, "Which deed is the best?" He said: "The remembrance of Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in a way that is best﴾ that he said: "[It is] 'There is no god but Allah.'"

al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The People of the Book used to recite the Torah in Hebrew and explain it to the People of Islam in Arabic. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Do not believe the People of the Book, nor disbelieve them, but say: We believe in what has been revealed to us and what has been revealed to you, and our God and your God is One, and to Him we are submitting.'"

al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, al-Daylami, and Abu Nasr al-Sijzi in al-Ibanah narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not ask the People of the Book about anything, for they will not guide you, and they have gone astray. Either you will affirm something false, or you will deny something true. By Allah, if Musa were alive among you, it would not be lawful for him except to follow me."

'Abd al-Razzaq and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Do not ask the People of the Book," and he mentioned something similar to the hadith of Jabir, then said: "If you must ask them, then look at what agrees with the Book of Allah and take it, and what contradicts the Book of Allah and leave it."
